summary: The ESA Amendments Act of 2025 reauthorizes the Endangered Species Act through fiscal year 2031, renames it to the Endangered Species Recovery Act, and generally narrows protections and requirements under the law. It establishes a National Listing Work Plan for scheduling species reviews, incentivizes private conservation through agreements, changes critical habitat designation rules, alters the federal consultation process, and adjusts judicial review and attorneys' fee caps.

affected_groups.effect: Can voluntarily enter into Conservation Benefit Agreements to avoid future land restrictions if a species is listed, and face modified critical habitat designations and streamlined permit processes.

Given opportunities to develop recovery strategies, submit data for species determinations, manage certain recovered threatened species, and receive notification of large critical habitat designations.
Must create a National Listing Work Plan, prepare economic and exclusion analyses for critical habitat designations, publish scientific data online, and report expenditures and litigation costs.
affected_groups.group: Federal Wildlife Agencies (Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service)

affected_groups.effect: Subject to capped attorneys' and expert witness fees ($125 per hour, $200,000 total) and limits on fee recovery if they have sought fees in three or more instances within a 12-month period.
affected_groups.group: Plaintiffs in Endangered Species Act Lawsuits

key_provisions: Reauthorizes appropriations for the Endangered Species Act through fiscal year 2031 and renames the law the Endangered Species Recovery Act.

Directs the Fish and Wildlife Service and the National Marine Fisheries Service to submit a National Listing Work Plan establishing a five-year schedule for addressing listing petitions and critical habitat designations, eliminating the 12-month deadline to act on listing petitions.

Provides statutory authority for Conservation Benefit Agreements, allowing private landowners and other parties to voluntarily reduce threats to candidate species in exchange for assurances that no additional land or resource restrictions will be imposed if the species is later listed.

Limits what land may be designated as critical habitat, exempts certain private lands covered by qualifying management plans, and exempts the approval of Conservation Benefit Agreements and incidental take permits from National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA) review.
Restricts protections for threatened species by tying regulation stringency to incremental recovery goals and allowing states to manage species under approved recovery strategies.

Limits attorneys' and expert witness fees in citizen suits to a maximum of $125 per hour and $200,000 total per suit, restricting awards to eligible parties meeting specific net worth and employee thresholds.

Modifies federal agency consultation requirements under Section 7 by narrowing what qualifies as an effect of an action, restricting reasonable and prudent measures, and setting rules for successive consultations.
missing_information: Specific economic outcomes or exact cost-benefit figures beyond the authorized appropriation amounts ($287,978,000 annually for species conservation, plus smaller amounts for other categories through FY2031).
summary_detail.plain_summary: The ESA Amendments Act of 2025 reauthorizes the Endangered Species Act through fiscal year 2031, renames it to the Endangered Species Recovery Act, and generally narrows protections and requirements under the law. It establishes a National Listing Work Plan for scheduling species reviews, incentivizes private conservation through agreements, changes critical habitat designation rules, alters the federal consultation process, and adjusts judicial review and attorneys' fee caps.
summary_detail.significance: The bill represents a major legislative modification to the primary U.S. wildlife conservation statute by shifting emphasis toward voluntary private landowner agreements, narrowing habitat protections, introducing fixed multi-year work plans for species listings, and limiting legal challenges and fee awards.
